I then bought five 3.5 inch SATA disk drive hot swap trays. I installed the 3 TB drives into the hot swap trays. I loaded my home brew server with five 3 TB disk drives. Using the Rocket RAID hard ware software I configured the five 3 TB drives into a RAID 5 configuration. This gave me 12 TB of RAID protected online storage. I also then installed two 100/1000 MB Ethernet adapter in a PCI slots. This gives me three independent Ethernet ports. (Two on adapters and one on the motherboard)

Here is where the problem occurred. I tried about 6 or 8 Linux distributions and none of them would recognize the RAID 5 Disk array so it came back with NO DRIVE FOUND for installation. I loaded my old standby Windows Server 2003 and had my server up and running. Since then I have added a external Utrium LTO-4 TAPE drive running on an external SAS port. (Not on the Rocket RAID) So I have 12 TB of Disk storage and can back it up to 1.6 TB external tape.

The preexisting condition rule is the worst facet of the ACA. It's the primary driver for insurance costs going through the roof because it's antithetical to the concept of insurance (e.g. you cant wait until after you crash your car to buy collision coverage).

The reason we had to put that in was because insurance companies were dumping people making big claims and saying that the person had hid a pre-existing condition from the insurance company. In short they took premiums from people for years and then refused to provide coverage when their customers tried to use the supposed service. We wouldn't have to put that in had we not been fucked by the insurance companies already. The idea is that this way there's no work around for the insurance companies.

Which is why they have the lapse penalty in this legislation. No coverage for more than 63 days? You're not going to be denied insurance, but you will be charged a 30% higher premium for a year.

Ultimately, the important thing here is that it makes health savings accounts and insurance unions (same exact concept as a credit union, just for healthcare instead of loans) feasible and attractive prospects. The biggest hurdle Obamacare faced was that it ripped people's existing plans out from under them. These days, nobody actually likes their plan unless they're indigent, and hopefully, many will shift to HSAs and insurance unions. These greedy bastards don't deserve our business anyway.

Another part I like about it is the tax credit system. A tax cut is a tax cut, and it'll help millions of Americans afford insurance while ripping what amounts to entitlements away from the willfully unemployed and doing no further harm to the disabled.

It's not a terrible plan by federal standards, especially since it reads like a temporary fix. This is their way to wind down Obamacare and the bullshit insurance industry. After we right the ship, we move it toward the real goal: a legitimate free market in this particular industry, just as we should strive to accomplish across the board.
